Our study area is mainly located in a forest mosaic landscape comprised by woodlands, grasslands, farmlands, and bare ground during the vegetation growing season on the south bank of this river. With a temperate continental climate, natural tree species growing widely on the banks of the Irtysh River mainly include Populus laurifolia Ledeb., Populus alba L., and Populus nigra L., and such riparian forests are regarded as an important gene pool for plants in the family Salicaceae. [prose] Three ecological traits that characterised functional diversity between ground beetle species included: body size (large vs. small), feeding trait (carnivorous vs. omnivorous), and wing morphology (macropterous vs. brachypterous) (Homburg et al., 2014) (Supporting Information Table S1). Body length was used as a measure of body size, which was measured as the distance from the tip of the mandibles to the end of the abdomen. Carabid species with an average body size equal to or longer than 15 mm were considered large; otherwise, they were considered small (Gobbi et al., 2007). Carabid species were considered carnivorous if they were strictly predators during their life cycle, whereas species that were occasional predators or herbivores were considered omnivorous (Gobbi & Fontaneto, 2008). For wing morphology, macropterous species were those with wings longer than the elytra, whereas brachypterous species were those with wings shorter than the elytra (Brambilla & Gobbi, 2014). Carabid FD was measured by calculating Rao’s quadratic entropy $( \mathrm { F D } _ { \mathrm { Q } } )$ , which is a multi-trait FD metric that describes the diversity of a given community, combining the relative abundances of species with the biological information about the functional differences between species (Rao, 1982; Ricotta, 2005). $\mathrm { F D } _ { \mathbf { Q } }$ expresses the average functional dissimilarity between two randomly selected individuals if relative abundance is calculated from the number of individuals, and it has been widespread used to characterise human impacts on ecosystem processes (Aubin et al., 2013). As DBH is often used as a proxy of tree height in most tree species, we only considered DBH as measure of tree size, which is an important structural trait, critical in forest ecology and for above ground biomass estimate. Canopy cover was assessed at four continuous 10 m  10 m assessment areas along the transect using a visual cover method (Humphrey et al., 1999). Percentage of vegetation cover on each plot was calculated from 10 random $1 \; \mathrm { { m } } \times 1$ m quadrats along the transect (Rahman et al., 2015). We also measured species richness and average height of herbaceous plant species in three random $5 \mathrm { ~ m ~ } \times 5$ m sampling subplots within each sampling plot. An important environmental factor, the nearest distance from the centre of sampling plot to river bank (the distance to river, Magagula, 2003; Rykken et al., 2007) was measured by using ENVI version 5.4 based on satellite images.
